en.biology: A heritable trait that increases an organism's fitness within a given environment, shaped by natural selection over generations.

3-5.classroomInstantiation: Natural selection simulation with beads; comparing beak shapes in Darwin's finches to available food types; explaining why dark coloring is common in pocket mice on dark lava rock.
3-5.educatorBridgingNote: At 3–5, 'adaptation' is named explicitly for the first time. Flag the intentionality misconception immediately. Cultural adaptations (tools, farming practices) can be introduced here as spreading by learning rather than by genes.
3-5.studentFacingDescription: Some traits help organisms survive and reproduce better than others. Over many generations, those helpful traits become more common — that process is called natural selection.

6-8.classroomInstantiation: Tracking allele frequency change across simulated generations; comparing cultural adaptation rates (fast) to genetic adaptation rates (slow).
6-8.educatorBridgingNote: Distinguish adaptation (the process) from an adaptation (a trait that resulted from selection). Cultural adaptations spread faster than genetic ones because they spread by learning.
6-8.studentFacingDescription: Adaptation happens at the population level — the change in how common a trait is across a population over generations.

9-12.classroomInstantiation: Separating adaptive evolution (selection) from non-adaptive evolution (drift, mutation); evaluating competing adaptive hypotheses for human life history evolution.
9-12.educatorBridgingNote: Students should ask: 'What is the evidence this trait was shaped by selection rather than drift?' — the empirical questions of adaptationism.
9-12.studentFacingDescription: Adaptation is one of several evolutionary mechanisms — selection, drift, mutation, and migration all shape trait frequencies. Only selection produces adaptation.

K-2.classroomInstantiation: Polar bears have thick fur for cold places; desert animals can go a long time without water; humans in cold climates historically wore many layers of clothing.
K-2.educatorBridgingNote: At K–2, adaptation is 'features that help' — functional and concrete. Do not introduce natural selection yet. Critically, do NOT frame adaptation as intentional; use passive constructions ('polar bears that had thicker fur were better able to survive').
K-2.studentFacingDescription: Animals and plants have features that help them survive in their home — different places need different features.
